title: Chapter IX

teacherSummary.text: Tormented by guilt, Victor considers suicide. His family withdraws to Belrive. Victor journeys into the Alps toward Chamounix, where the majesty of mountains, glaciers and Mont Blanc offers temporary relief.

vocabulary.context: I passed the bridge of Pélissier, where the ravine, which the river forms, opened before me, and I began to ascend the mountain that overhangs it.

vocabulary.definition: To cause to rest by soothing influences
vocabulary.context: The same lulling sounds acted as a lullaby to my too keen sensations: when I placed my head upon my pillow, sleep crept over me; I felt it as it came, and blessed the giver of oblivion.

context.history: The Vale of Chamounix and Mont Blanc were Romantic pilgrimage sites; Percy Shelley wrote 'Mont Blanc' (1816).

significance: The sublime landscape mirrors Victor's mind: grand, cold and overwhelming.
discussionQuestions: How does the mountain landscape reflect Victor's feelings?
Where does setting appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with the sublime power of nature?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter IX,” how does Shelley show despair and the sublime? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the setting you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter IX develops the idea of despair and the sublime. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of setting and imagery shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses setting in Chapter IX to complicate the reader's understanding of despair and the sublime. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter IX within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of despair and the sublime responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter IX as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of despair and the sublime. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

satQuestions.passage: Our house was the house of mourning. My father’s health was deeply shaken by the horror of the recent events. Elizabeth was sad and desponding; she no longer took delight in her ordinary occupations; all pleasure seemed to her sacrilege toward the dead; eternal woe and tears she then thought was the just tribute she should pay to innocence so blasted and destroyed. She was no longer that happy creature, who in earlier youth wandered with me on the banks of the lake, and talked with ecstasy of our future prospects. The first of those sorrows which are sent to wean us from the earth, had visited her, and its dimming influence quenched her dearest smiles.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter IX”?

segments.activity: Quick-write and share on the opening question.
segments.script: Good morning, readers. Before we open the book, take three minutes and write your honest answer to this: How does the mountain landscape reflect Victor's feelings? There is no wrong answer yet; we will test our ideas against the text today.

segments.activity: Model pronouncing, defining and using five key words in context.
segments.script: Today's words include overhangs, lulling, glaciers, perpetrate, avalanche. Watch how I figure out a word from its sentence before I check the dictionary. Here is the line: “I passed the bridge of Pélissier, where the ravine, which the river forms, opened before me, and I began to ascend the mountain that overhangs it.” My guess comes from the clues around it; the dictionary says: To impend or hang over.

segments.activity: Present background, then the significance of the chapter.
segments.script: Let me give you some background that the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. The Vale of Chamounix and Mont Blanc were Romantic pilgrimage sites; Percy Shelley wrote 'Mont Blanc' (1816). Now, why does this chapter matter? The sublime landscape mirrors Victor's mind: grand, cold and overwhelming. As you listen, jot one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Setting, Imagery, Tone / mood.
segments.script: Let's read this passage together. I will read the first sentence; you track along. Every time you spot setting, mark it. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice here? I will collect three ideas on the board and we will choose the strongest one together, using the evidence.
